paper_title: One Bias Score, Two Factors: How Mitigations Affect Option Bias in Multiple-Choice Evaluation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reordering multiple-choice options can change a model's answer, an effect studied as selection bias (a preference for certain option letters) and as order sensitivity (changes in answers across option orderings). We connect these perspectives through the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), which measures how unevenly option letters are selected across questions and orderings. When every option of each question appears equally often at each position, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two label-free factors: the flip rate and the positional skew. The flip rate is the fraction of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings; the positional skew is the standard deviation of option-letter selection rates among those questions. Across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate tracks accuracy and output uncertainty, while the positional skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior. Prior correction for selection bias mainly reduces the positional skew. Aggregating each ordering with its reversal, a mitigation for order sensitivity, mainly reduces the flip rate. Both reduce the range of accuracy across correct-answer letters by similar amounts, but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals. Applying prior correction before aggregation reduces both factors and further narrows this accuracy range. However, aggregation lowers the flip rate partly by settling questions on the same wrong option. We therefore recommend reporting both factors to distinguish mitigation effects, alongside accuracy to distinguish stability from correctness.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multiple-choice evaluation of language models depends on the order in which the options are presented. Multiple-choice benchmarks rank models by how often they select the correct option, assuming that models choice depends on what the options say, not on where they appear. Yet reordering the options, without changing which answer is correct, can change model selections enough to alter these rankings (Alzahrani et al., 2024). Two concerns organise the work on this effect, which we call option bias. Selection bias is preference for certain options by their letter (the option symbol: A, B, C, . . . ); it is summarised with statistics pooled over benchmarks answers and reduced by prior correction, which divides out an estimated option-symbol prior (Zheng et al., 2024; Reif and Schwartz, 2024), or by intervening on the model (Choi et al., 2025). Order sensitivity is the change of an answer with the order; it is counted per item (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Li et al., 2024a) and handled by aggregation over several orderings (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Wei et al., 2024). Selection bias is thus read over pooled answers, order sensitivity per question. Mitigation methods are commonly compared by pooled bias score (e.g., Zheng et al., 2024; Choi et al., 2025): single number computed over all of benchmarks answers that grows as the answers concentrate on some letters or as accuracy varies across them. One such score is the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), the standard deviation across letters of each letters share of the answers. Two methods with similar gains can change different parts of option bias. Take one method from each line of work. prior correction divides each letters probability by an estimate of how much the model favours that letter whatever option it holds (Zheng et al., 2024); an aggregation asks each question in given order and in its reverse and picks the option whose two probabilities have the largest product (Wei et al., 2024). 1 (a) What flip is. It also leaves fewer reversals of model rankings than the correction, and it lowers flips partly by settling questions on wrong answer. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: We discuss the most relevant literature here and provide broader discussion in Section G. Selection bias and prior correction. Zheng et al. (2024) define selection bias as preference for certain option symbols (option IDs in their terms), identify prior over ID tokens as primary contributor alongside modeland task-dependent position effects, and measure it with RStd, the SD of classwise recalls, under the premise that correct answers are randomly placed. Their PriDe estimates the prior from permutations of few items and divides it out of the rest; they combine it with partial permutation averaging and relate the estimated prior to option-position recalls. Related corrections prune bias nodes or add an auxiliary option (Choi et al., 2025), intervene on attention heads and feed-forward vectors (Zhou et al., 2024b), or correct label priors in in-context classification, where content-free estimates can hurt (Fei et al., 2023; Reif and Schwartz, 2024). Guda et al. (2025) observe that, on average, PriDe lowers RStd but raises other measures, evaluating pooled and per-item measures together. We distinguish the quantities measured and the operations applied rather than assigning each paper one perspective, and show which factor of pooled score correction moves. Order sensitivity and aggregation. Order sensitivity is conjectured to arise from an interaction between uncertainty among models leading choices and question-dependent positional preferences, with the uncertainty part supported by GPT-4 answer probabilities and accuracy improved by majority vote over reorderings (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024). Wei et al. (2024) measure two-ordering fluctuation rate, find more fluctuation on subtasks with lower accuracy in most tested models, and multiply each contents probabilities under an ordering and its reversal; they also study probability calibration. Inconsistency under answer-preserving perturbations has been read as sign that single-format scores overstate knowledge and built into scoring (Li et al., 2024a; Gupta et al., 2025), or reported as reliability beside accuracy (Cocchieri et al., 2026). These measures count changes under their chosen perturbations; we relate the flip rate to pooled scores under balanced design and show that which orderings an aggregation pairs changes whether it also lowers the skew. Reporting both quantities. LLM-judge audits report how often an order effect occurs beside which position it favours (Shi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024a), and for two candidates the raw fairness score of Shi et al. (2025) already combines the two. We give the exact factorisation of the pooled SD under any balanced ordering design for multiple-choice evaluation and use it to read what mitigation operations change.

sections.title: 4 Experimental setup
sections.content: Models and benchmarks. We evaluate 41 open-weight checkpoints from seven model families, pretrained and post-trained, on 12 benchmarks with two, four or ten options, such as PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), five-subject subset of MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024b). cell is one checkpointbenchmark pair; correlations across cells count each once. Readouts. The answer is the option letter with the highest next-token probability, the first-token readout. Five-shot prompting, and direct-answer and chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) with greedy decoding, serve as checks. Mitigation operations. The operations rework the stored letter probabilities and are compared on the same items. Prior correction divides every querys letter probabilities by an option-symbol prior, the models preference for each letter, estimated on held-out 5% of cells items as in PriDes reported setting: PriDes estimate (Zheng et al., 2024) or the mean letter probability, variant of batch calibration (Zhou et al., 2024a). Aggregation multiplies, for each content, its probabilities under the presented ordering and under its reversal, the probability product of Wei et al. (2024), which we call the reversal product, and returns the content with the largest product. composition applies two operations in sequence, chiefly correction and then the product. Every operation returns one answer per cyclic ordering, and both factors are computed over these answers. Statistics. Correlations are Spearman (rs) unless stated otherwise, and differences between conditions on the same cells carry 95% checkpoint-block intervals, which resample whole checkpoints. Section gives the full protocol.

sections.content: This section shows that the two factors of the identity record different behaviour.

Within cell, flips concentrate on items whose two leading options are close in probability under the canonical order, sign of output uncertainty: smaller gap marks flipping rather than stable items with median AUC of 0.85. This holds even among items wrong under every ordering, so it is not accuracy in disguise. Pezeshkpour and Hruschka (2024) conjecture such uncertainty behind order sensitivity; whether the models internal uncertainty causes the flips is left to future work. low flip rate still does not mean high accuracy: an item that keeps one wrong answer does not flip.

sections.title: 5.2 The skew reflects option-symbol bias
sections.content: Option-symbol bias is models preference for particular option letters, which PriDe estimates as prior over the letters (Zheng et al., 2024). We estimate this prior on the held-out 5% of cells items and measure the skew on the rest, and three results tie the two together. Models with more uneven prior have larger skew, also given accuracy. The flipping answers lean towards the letters the prior favours (median centred cosine 0.87 on four-option cells, against 0.10 for the prior with its letters permuted). And dividing the prior out lowers the skew while the flip rate barely moves, whereas dividing out the permuted prior raises it (Figure 4). The skew is where models option-symbol bias shows in the changing answers; under cyclic orderings this letter preference is also position preference. Both factors are reliable: each ranks the cells nearly the same way on two random halves of their items, and the two carry comparable shares of the variance of the log pooled SD across cells. Section gives these analyses, the canonical-order gap and the controls on the flip rate.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Under balanced orderings, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two behaviours: the flip rate, how often the order changes an answer, and the positional skew, how unevenly the changed answers land; balanced RStd shares only the flip rate unless = 2. Mitigation methods move these behaviours differently and leave different harms. Prior correction mainly lowers the skew and aggregating an ordering with its reversal mainly the flip rate; the two narrow the placement range by similar amounts, yet on the same cells the aggregation leaves fewer rank reversals and lowers flips partly by settling items on wrong answer. correction followed by the aggregation lowers both factors. lower factor alone is therefore not evidence of better model. Flips also track accuracy and output uncertainty, and the skew tracks the models optionsymbol bias. Both factors come from one sweep over the orderings without gold labels; we recommend reporting them with accuracy and judging mitigation method by all three and by the harm of interest.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our analysis characterises the observable effects of option order, but not the model-internal mechanisms that produce them. The prior corrections and controlled interventions act on output scores, and the observed associations with accuracy and output uncertainty do not establish causal explanations. Moreover, although the pooling identity is exact under balanced orderings, reducing either factor does not guarantee better predictions: consistently wrong answers can remain stable, and changes in positional skew need not translate into improved placement robustness or ranking stability. Our experiments also focus on deterministic readouts of mostly English multiple-choice benchmarks and specific mitigation configurations. Future work should investigate the internal mechanisms underlying the two factors through targeted interventions and theoretically characterise when reductions in each factor lead to improvements in correctness and evaluation stability.

sections.content: This section gives the protocol of the mitigation operations in Sections 6 and 7, the decomposition of the letter preference that the reversal product averages, and each operations effects. 23 D.1 Protocol All operations use the same first-token predictions, items and orderings. Each comparison uses calibration split of 5% of each cells items, at least one, and evaluates every operation on the remaining 95%; no gold label enters any prior or operation. The cohort is the cells with at least three options, each scored under its cyclic orderings and their reversals. Each item is presented in its cyclic orderings; in our protocol an operation may query further orderings provided no two presented orderings share query, and every statistic is computed over the answers, each counted at the letter that holds the chosen content in its presented ordering. Comparisons of the corrections alone use every first-token cell, two-option cells included. The prior experiment of Section 5 uses the same split. Prior correction. PriDes prior is estimated on the calibration items: for each of them the normalised geometric mean over the orderings of its option-letter probabilities, averaged over those items (Zheng et al., 2024). It is divided out of every ordering of the evaluated items; when cell is scored on its canonical ordering alone the prior is applied to that ordering only. The published method instead scores the estimation items by permutation averaging and the remaining items in their default ordering, and averages over five splits. Batch calibration divides by the mean letter probability over the estimation items orderings, an arithmetic-mean variant of the log-score correction of Zhou et al. (2024a), which estimates over the test batch; variants that average log probabilities, or estimate over all test items, move both factors the same way. Neither correction adds an option, and the argmax is over the original K. Aggregation. The probability product multiplies, for each content, its probabilities under the presented ordering and under that orderings reversal and returns the content with the largest product, following the forward and backward pairing of Wei et al. (2024); exact ties go to the earliest letter of the presented ordering. The reversal of cyclic ordering is not cyclic for 3, so the partners of different presented orderings are distinct. majority vote over fixed pool of orderings (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024), with ties broken by content rather than by presented position, returns one content for every presented ordering; its flip rate, pooled SD and balanced RStd are zero by construction, and with no flipping item its skew is undefined; the convention = unif at FL = 0 in Section is algebraic, not an estimate of that skew. We therefore treat the vote as the zero-flip case and compare prior correction with the reversal product on the factors. Compositions and controls. composition applies correction and then an aggregation to the corrected probabilities; composing two corrections re-estimates the second prior on the first ones output. The letterpermuted control divides by the estimated prior after permuting its letters, every non-identity permutation for four options, the swap for two and distinct non-identity permutations drawn uniformly at random for ten, and averages the result. The canonical margin is the gap between the two largest letter probabilities under π0 alone. Rank reversals count the checkpoint pairs on benchmark whose accuracy difference changes sign across the presented cyclic orderings, on the items shared by all of them; counting each pair on the items its two checkpoints share instead lowers every level, and the compositions difference from the reversal product stays unresolved under both counts. composition is compared with each of its components on the same cells, with paired checkpoint-block intervals. sections.title: G Closest related measurements and mitigations
sections.content: This section extends the comparisons of Section 2 to the closest measurements and mitigations. Consistency measures for multiple choice. Cocchieri et al. (2026) define ReCon over seven input formats, including open answers mapped back to the options. Its complement counts any inconsistency on that variant set, so it is analogous to, but not numerically identical to, the cyclic flip rate. Their high multiple-choice scores with lower cross-format consistency do not contradict the flip cap, which bounds the flip rate by accuracy averaged over the same evaluated variants. Gupta et al. (2025) count an item as correct only when it is answered correctly under both the original and shuffled order. SCORE (Nalbandyan et al., 2025) reports pairwise consistency rate under reordered choices, paraphrased prompts and sampling seeds beside mean accuracy and accuracy ranges across those perturbations, and finds consistency correlated with mean accuracy across models, as the flip rate and accuracy are in our panel. Consistency without correctness is also recognised. Li et al. (2024b) find that consistency over repeated queries need not imply correctness, and Cocchieri et al. (2026) report ReCon beside ReAcc, which also requires every answer to be correct. Their repeated-query analysis is within items, whereas our association with accuracy is across cells under cyclic reordering, and it likewise does not say whether an individual stable answer is correct. We carry the distinction to mitigation, measuring whether the items that stop flipping become stably correct or stably wrong. Consistency and position preference are already reported together. Judge audits report position consistency, how often verdict survives swap, beside direction score built to shrink towards zero as consistency rises (Shi et al., 2025), or swap-conflict rate beside position-conditioned win rates (Wang et al., 2024a). The raw fairness score of Shi et al. (2025) already combines how often pair is judged inconsistently with the direction of the preference among those pairs. For two candidates without ties it follows from their definition that its absolute value, divided by the number of swapped pairs, is twice the pooled selection-rate SD; their final, normalised score is different quantity. Both audits also find inconsistency more frequent when the two candidates are close in quality, measured through scores or win rates, and Shi et al. (2025) report preferred positions that reverse with the task. The canonical margin of Section 5 is related but different measure of uncertainty, and neither identifies missing knowledge as cause. In multiple choice, Guda et al. (2025) evaluate per-item and pooled measures together and find that mitigation gain depends on the measure: averaged over their models and datasets, PriDe lowers RStd while raising the Permutation Bias Metric (PBM) and CKLD, whereas their consistency-oriented fine-tuning lowers PBM without lowering CKLD. The pooling identity makes this combination exact for the pooled selection-rate SD under any balanced multiple-choice design, with correction for unbalanced designs and an upper bound for the KL divergence from uniform. 30 Gold-dependent measures: RStd and CKLD. RStd (Zheng et al., 2024) and CKLD (Choi et al., 2025) compare predictions with gold labels, through classwise recalls and the gold answer distribution. The pooled statistics we compare are label-free analogues computed from selection frequencies against uniform. The selection-rate SD factors through the chosen-position profile g; RStd evaluated with every items correct option balanced across positions factors through the gold-dependent profile instead, and canonical-order RStd has no such identity (Section 3.3). Choi et al. (2025) observe sharper choice imbalance among incorrect answers and transfer bias vectors taken from hidden states across datasets. Our partition instead splits the items by whether their choice stays the same under reordering, which yields an exact identity under balanced orderings, and we do not identify their hidden-state bias vector with the option-symbol prior. Corrections and direction. PriDe (Zheng et al., 2024) estimates prior on each of few estimation items and applies the average of these priors to the remaining items, so its correction is itself pooled. It uses permutations of the estimation items to cancel the content terms in log probabilities under its multiplicative, order-invariant model, whereas the pooling identity counts choices and needs no probability model. Dividing by an estimated shared prior does not enforce agreement across orderings, although exact prior removal under PriDes assumptions would recover an order-invariant content distribution. Zheng et al. (2026) train for agreement across orderings with permutation-aware GRPO that rewards answers matching the unique most frequent choice over permutation group. That reward acts on what the flip rate counts, whereas the PriDe reductions we split come mostly from the skew.
